summary: This document specifies DOTS signal channel Call Home, where a Call Home DOTS server starts a secure connection to a Call Home DOTS client and receives attack traffic information from it. The server uses that to identify compromised devices launching outgoing DDoS attacks and mitigate them. It is not limited to home networks.

eli5.summary: Usually a victim calls for help during an attack. Here the helper calls the victim to learn what attack traffic looks like, so it can stop the bad devices that are sending it.

questions: stop outgoing ddos attacks closer to source
how to stop outbound ddos attacks
dots signal channel call home explained
what is a call home dots server
subtitle: How a network that hosts attack sources can call its provider back, so outbound DDoS traffic is blocked near where it starts.

tldr.problem: The base DOTS signal channel only helps a network that is being attacked. It has no way for an ISP to ask a customer network to stop a compromised device that is attacking someone else.
tldr.mechanism: The DOTS server in the source network opens the (D)TLS connection to the provider's DOTS client, reversing the usual (D)TLS roles. The client then sends mitigation requests that name the attack sources, and the server finds and blocks the compromised device.
tldr.outcome: Attack traffic can be stopped closer to its source without altering legitimate traffic. The request is advisory: the Call Home DOTS server and its administrator decide what to do.

today: RFC 9066 is a Proposed Standard from December 2021. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the base protocol in RFC 9132.

sections.title: Stopping Attacks at Their Source
sections.content:
The DOTS signal channel in RFC 9132 tells a mitigator that a network is under a Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack. It only covers inbound attacks. It does not cover controlling attacks close to the sources that are misusing network resources, which are outbound DDoS attacks.

An ISP may be able to see outgoing attack traffic from its subscribers, but the DOTS signal channel gives it no way to ask for that traffic to be blocked close to the source without altering legitimate traffic. DOTS signal channel Call Home (DOTS Call Home) fills that gap.

Appendix A explains why this matters for homes. Internet of Things devices are often compromised, are hard to upgrade, and the owner does not know. An ISP behind a NAT usually cannot tell which device in a home network is generating the traffic, but a security function in the home can.

The RFC notes that it considered a different design, with a new attribute on the existing channel and a DOTS server in the source network. It rejected it in part because opening a channel toward a source network is complicated by translators and firewalls, and because that DOTS server would be exposed to fingerprinting and DoS attacks.
sections.eli5: If a toy robot in your house is smashing things next door, the neighbour can already shout for help. This RFC lets the neighbour's helper phone your house and say which robot to switch off.

sections.title: Roles and Deployment Scope
sections.content:
Call Home DOTS agents otherwise keep the DOTS roles from RFC 8612. The Call Home DOTS server sits in the domain that hosts the attack source. The Call Home DOTS client sits upstream, for example at a provider running a DDoS Mitigation System (DMS). The client learns about an attack from deployment-specific triggers such as an alert from an attack target or a transit provider. The RFC does not define those triggers.

A typical Call Home DOTS server is enabled on a Customer Premises Equipment (CPE), though it can also run on a border router or a dedicated appliance. Despite the home-network examples, the RFC says the solution is not specific to home networks and also targets enterprise networks, transit networks and data centers.

The Call Home channel does not require or preclude the base DOTS signal channel. A network can run both, with the same or distinct DMS providers, and one node can host both a DOTS client and a Call Home DOTS server. The Call Home option does require the DMS provider to be on the default forwarding path of the network's outbound traffic.

Call Home DOTS servers must be provisioned with a way to reach the upstream client, for example through RFC 8973. A Call Home DOTS server keeps a single signal channel session for each DOTS-capable upstream provisioning domain.
sections.eli5: The house has a little helper box that dials out to the provider. The provider can then talk back to the house through that open line.

sections.title: The Call Home Procedure
sections.content:
Only one thing changes compared with RFC 9132: the roles at the (D)TLS layer reverse. The Call Home DOTS server acts as the DTLS or TLS client, and the Call Home DOTS client acts as the DTLS or TLS server. With UDP the server starts a DTLS connection. With TCP it opens the TCP connection and then starts TLS. Happy Eyeballs from RFC 9132 is used when initiating connections.

Existing certificate chains and mutual authentication are unaffected. Because many Call Home DOTS servers may be involved, the RFC encourages automating the provisioning of their credentials.

Once connected, the Call Home DOTS client may request, withdraw or retrieve the status of mitigation requests over this connection. Peers may agree on a specific port, by configuration or by discovery.

Heartbeats differ from the base protocol. The Call Home DOTS client fetches session configuration, and the server adjusts heartbeat-interval to fit NAT and firewall binding timers. Keeping those bindings alive is the server's responsibility. If an outgoing attack saturates the server's link, the client MUST keep using the channel even if it hears nothing from the server. If the server receives traffic from the client, it MUST keep using the channel even when missing-hb-allowed is reached. If it hears nothing for that whole span, it concludes the session is disconnected and MUST try to establish a new one, preferably by resuming the (D)TLS session.
sections.eli5: The house dials the provider and keeps the line warm with regular little pings. If the line goes dead, the house calls again.

sections.title: Mitigation Requests and Redirection
sections.content:
The mitigation request of RFC 9132 is extended with attack source information: source-prefix (a list of attacker IP prefixes), source-port-range (lower and upper port numbers) and source-icmp-type-range (lower and upper ICMP types). In a Call Home request source-prefix is mandatory and target-prefix MUST be included. The prefix list MUST NOT include broadcast, loopback or multicast addresses, and the client MUST check that the prefixes belong to the server's domain.

The client SHOULD add port or ICMP type ranges to tell apart nodes that share a prefix. IPv6 prefixes are usually enough to identify an endpoint on their own. Only immediate mitigation requests are allowed: a request with trigger-mitigation set to false MUST be rejected with 4.00 (Bad Request).

The server MUST check that the source prefix is in its domain. It may ask an administrator for consent. If it does, it replies 2.01 (Created) with status 1 (attack-mitigation-in-progress), and later reports status 2 (attack-successfully-mitigated) once blocked. If the traffic is judged legitimate, the request is rejected with 4.09 (Conflict) or a new conflict-clause value of 4.

A Call Home DOTS server MUST NOT support the base redirected signaling (a 5.03 response), and a client MUST silently discard one. Instead, a client that wants to send the server to another Call Home DOTS client sends a Non-confirmable PUT to .well-known/dots/redirect with alt-ch-client (mandatory), alt-ch-client-record and ttl (both optional). The server answers 2.01 (Created), closes the connection and connects to the new client.
sections.eli5: The provider tells the house which address and which kind of traffic looks bad, and the house checks the claim before it acts. If the provider wants the house to call a different helper, it can say so.

sections.title: Address Sharing and Port Choice
sections.content:
Address sharing makes it hard to point at one device. With a Carrier-Grade NAT between the domains, the Call Home DOTS server knows only the internal addresses. A client aware of an on-path CGN MUST NOT use the external address or port and MUST use the internal ones, and SHOULD use mechanisms such as RFC 8512 or RFC 8513 to find them. For NAT64 with an IPv4 target, the IPv4-converted IPv6 address SHOULD be used.

Where a MAP Border Relay or lwAFTR serves customers, the same IPv4 address is assigned to multiple customers, so identifying an attack source MUST also use source port numbers. When a NAT sits at the edge of the server's domain, such as in a CPE, the server looks up its NAT mapping table using the attack information as a key to find the internal device, which lets it isolate that device without disturbing other services.

Appendix B covers a case where a CPE runs both a base DOTS client and a Call Home DOTS server toward the same ISP. The RFC chooses a dedicated port number for Call Home over signaling the role through the data channel, because it is simpler and only costs a second (D)TLS session. The CPE uses port 4646 for the base channel, and the Call Home port can be configured locally or discovered, for example through RFC 8973.
sections.eli5: When many houses share one street address, the provider has to say which room the bad device is in. The house then looks up its own list to find the right gadget.

sections.title: The YANG Module and CBOR Keys
sections.content:
The module ietf-dots-call-home augments the ietf-dots-signal-channel module from RFC 9132 using the data structure extension of RFC 8791. It adds source-prefix, source-port-range and source-icmp-type-range to the mitigation scope, and a Call Home choice with alt-ch-client, alt-ch-client-record and ttl to the redirected signal.

Messages are encoded in CBOR, so each new parameter gets a key value. The new keys run from 32768 to 32775, and are registered as comprehension-optional values in the IANA DOTS Signal Channel CBOR Key Values registry. The YANG module also enforces that an upper port or ICMP type is greater than or equal to its lower bound.
sections.eli5: To keep messages small, each new field gets a short number as its name tag.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DOTS agents MUST authenticate each other using (D)TLS before a session is valid. Filters on the Call Home DOTS server can allow only the trusted client to reach it, which reduces exposure to scanning and DoS. Ordinary precautions against computationally expensive handshakes are recommended, such as temporarily adding a source to a drop-list after a set number of failed authentication attempts.

The biggest risk is a misbehaving client that labels legitimate traffic as attack traffic. Servers should not blindly trust requests. They could inspect traffic from the suspect device, redirect it to a scrubbing system instead of blocking all of it, or seek the administrator's consent. Requests that name internal-only addresses should be discarded absent explicit policy.

On privacy, the RFC says the protocol does not leak new information that eases surveillance. The server need not share local information such as internal identifiers, and the Call Home is only advisory: it does not impose any action in the network hosting the attacker. Misattribution is avoided by identifying the network to which a suspect source belongs.
sections.eli5: The house should not just do whatever the caller says. It checks first, and only the provider it trusts is allowed to call.

items.label: source-prefix
items.desc: Attacker IP prefixes (array of text strings).

items.label: source-port-range
items.desc: Ports used by the attack traffic (array).

items.desc: ICMP types used by the attack traffic (array).

items.desc: FQDN of an alternate Call Home DOTS client.

items.desc: IP addresses of the alternate client (array).

items.label: ttl
items.desc: How long the alternate client may be cached (unsigned).
